One enormous journey.

This version follows the complete route place by place — from Santiago through Patagonia, the Río de la Plata, the Altiplano, the Andes, Brazil’s Atlantic coast and finally the Colombian Caribbean.

where it all began · Chile
The complete route

A continent crossed again and again.

The route follows the journey in order, including the final loop from the Colombian Caribbean back to Santiago for a few more days, and then north again to Cartagena before Amsterdam. The distances shown are the shortest geographic line between each mapped point, so the real journey by road, bus, ferry, plane and trail was much longer.

Mapped minimum: ≈ 33,243 km Activities such as the W Trek, Inca Trail and Lost City Trek are described separately rather than artificially added to point-to-point distances.
01

Chile

From the capital to volcanoes, islands and Patagonia

≈ 4,580 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

01
0 km from the previous point

Santiago de Chile

Santiago was founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1541 beside the Mapocho River, on land inhabited long before the Spanish conquest. It grew from a colonial settlement into Chile’s political and economic centre, framed by the Andes and the Coastal Range. Because of that geography, Santiago can feel like several cities at once: dense historic neighbourhoods, modern business districts and mountain viewpoints all compressed into the same basin.

Little local gem ✦ Cerro San Cristóbal rises directly out of the city and is part of the huge Metropolitan Park, one of the largest urban parks in Latin America.

♡ This is where Maud’s Latin American journey began.

02
899 km from the previous point

Puerto Varas

Puerto Varas developed on the shore of Lake Llanquihue during the nineteenth-century German colonisation of southern Chile. Its wooden houses, gardens and food culture still reflect that history. The lakefront became a natural meeting point between farming communities, lake navigation and the routes leading deeper into Patagonia.

Little local gem ✦ on clear days the Osorno and Calbuco volcanoes dominate the view across Lake Llanquihue.

03
47 km from the previous point

Hike around Osorno Volcano

Osorno is a near-symmetrical stratovolcano that became one of the visual symbols of Chile’s Lake District. Its slopes lie within protected landscapes between Lakes Llanquihue and Todos los Santos. Its snowy cone has shaped the visual identity of the region for generations and is visible from an enormous part of the Llanquihue basin.

Little local gem ✦ the volcano reaches about 2,650 metres, and its almost perfect cone made early travellers compare it to Mount Fuji.

♡ Maud hiked around Osorno.

04
72 km from the previous point

Tagua Tagua

Tagua Tagua lies in the Puelo River basin, where temperate rainforest, granite mountains and glacial lakes form one of northern Patagonia’s most remote landscapes. The isolation is part of its character: the landscape feels less like a stop between towns and more like a deliberate departure from them.

Little local gem ✦ Parque Tagua Tagua is reached by crossing the lake and protects ancient alerce forest, waterfalls and mountain trails.

05
189 km from the previous point

Chiloé Island

Chiloé developed a distinctive island culture from the meeting of Indigenous traditions, Spanish settlement and centuries of maritime isolation. Its wooden architecture and seafaring culture remain central to its identity. Myths, fishing, potato cultivation and wooden churches all grew inside that island environment, giving Chiloé one of Chile’s strongest regional identities.

Little local gem ✦ sixteen of Chiloé’s wooden churches are UNESCO World Heritage sites, built through a tradition that blended European church forms with Chilote carpentry.

06
22 km from the previous point

Castro

Castro was founded in 1567 and is one of Chile’s oldest continuously inhabited colonial cities. It became an important centre of the Chiloé archipelago. The city works as both an island capital and a living showcase of Chilote architecture, with neighbourhoods stretching between steep hills and the sea.

Little local gem ✦ Castro is famous for its palafitos — brightly painted wooden houses standing on stilts along the tidal waterfront.

07
1,032 km from the previous point

Puerto Natales

Puerto Natales grew in the early twentieth century through sheep ranching and maritime trade in Última Esperanza. Today it is the main gateway to Torres del Paine. For decades it was tied to the huge sheep-estancia economy of southern Patagonia; today hikers from around the world pass through the same windswept port on their way to the mountains.

Little local gem ✦ its waterfront looks across a maze of fjords and channels toward the Patagonian Andes.

08
107 km from the previous point

W Trek · Torres del Paine

Torres del Paine National Park protects granite towers, glacial lakes, steppe and part of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field. The W Trek links several of the park’s most famous valleys. The trail repeatedly changes character — forest, exposed valleys, lakes and granite walls — which is why the distance alone never really captures what the route feels like.

Little local gem ✦ depending on the exact version, the W is roughly 70–80 km of hiking.

♡ Maud completed the W Trek.

41
2,212 km from the previous point

Santiago de Chile · return

Returning to Santiago made the city a recurring point in the route rather than simply its beginning. By this point Santiago was no longer simply the first pin on the map; returning to it gave the city an entirely different emotional place in the journey.

Little local gem ✦ from many parts of the city, fresh winter snow on the Andes can look almost impossibly close.

♡ Maud returned to Santiago later in the journey.

02

Argentina

Ice, granite and the long jump to Buenos Aires

≈ 3,377 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

09
105 km from the previous point

El Calafate

El Calafate began as a supply point for Patagonian sheep ranches and was officially founded in 1927. Its modern identity is inseparable from nearby Los Glaciares National Park. Its transformation from a small Patagonian settlement into an international travel base happened largely because the glaciers made this remote corner of Argentina a destination in its own right.

Little local gem ✦ the town takes its name from the calafate berry; a local saying claims that whoever eats it will return to Patagonia.

10
64 km from the previous point

Perito Moreno Glacier

Perito Moreno is one of the most famous outlet glaciers of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field. Unlike many glaciers worldwide, it has experienced long periods of relative stability. The glacier descends from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field into Lago Argentino, creating a wall of blue-white ice that can rise tens of metres above the water.

Little local gem ✦ when the glacier advances against the Magallanes Peninsula, it can dam part of Lago Argentino until the water eventually breaks through the ice.

♡ Here, an American couple paid for a boat tour that brought Maud close to the ice.

11
136 km from the previous point

Mount Fitz Roy

The granite peak known in Argentina as Cerro Fitz Roy rises above the border region of Patagonia. The Tehuelche name, Chaltén, is commonly understood as ‘smoking mountain’ because clouds often gather around the summit. Its silhouette is so closely associated with Patagonia that it appears in logos, photographs and climbing history far beyond the small town beneath it.

Little local gem ✦ the mountain is only 3,405 metres high, but its steep granite walls make it one of the world’s most technically demanding famous peaks.

12
13 km from the previous point

El Chaltén

El Chaltén is one of Argentina’s youngest towns, established in 1985 near the Chilean border. It later became known as the country’s trekking capital. The town is unusually intertwined with the surrounding landscape: streets simply turn into trails, and the peaks remain visible from almost everywhere.

Little local gem ✦ many of its best-known hikes begin directly from town, so hikers can leave their accommodation on foot without using a car.

13
2,022 km from the previous point

Buenos Aires

Buenos Aires was founded twice, in 1536 and 1580, and became the great port city of the Río de la Plata. Immigration, trade, tango and political life shaped its modern identity. Its neighbourhoods developed very different personalities — from the old port and immigrant districts to elegant nineteenth-century avenues and a huge café culture.

Little local gem ✦ Avenida 9 de Julio is one of the city’s great urban symbols, with the Obelisk standing at its centre.

16
1,037 km from the previous point

Iguazú Falls

The Iguazú River drops through a vast system of waterfalls shared by Argentina and Brazil, protected by national parks on both sides of the border. The falls sit inside subtropical forest, so the experience is not only the water itself but also heat, mist, vegetation and wildlife surrounding the walkways.

Little local gem ✦ the system contains roughly 275 separate falls depending on water level, with the Devil’s Throat as its most famous section.

BONUS

Uruguay

Across the Río de la Plata

≈ 212 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

14
51 km from the previous point

Colonia del Sacramento

Colonia was founded by the Portuguese in 1680 and repeatedly changed hands between Portugal and Spain. Its historic quarter preserves the physical layers of that contested frontier history. Portuguese and Spanish architectural traditions overlap in a very compact historic centre, which makes walking through it feel like moving between two colonial worlds.

Little local gem ✦ its old street plan is irregular and Portuguese in character, unlike the strict Spanish colonial grids common elsewhere in the region.

15
161 km from the previous point

Montevideo

Montevideo was founded by the Spanish in the eighteenth century as a strategic port facing Portuguese expansion. It later became the capital of independent Uruguay. The city grew around its port but developed an unusually relaxed relationship with the water, with beaches and public spaces forming part of everyday urban life.

Little local gem ✦ La Rambla, the waterfront road and promenade, runs for more than 20 km along the Río de la Plata and is central to daily city life.

03

Paraguay

One city — and then a very long bus ride

≈ 319 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

17
319 km from the previous point

Asunción

Founded in 1537, Asunción became an early Spanish base for the colonisation of the Río de la Plata interior and later the capital of Paraguay. The city carries visible layers of colonial history, nineteenth-century wars and twentieth-century political life, all along the Paraguay River.

Little local gem ✦ it is often called the ‘Mother of Cities’ because expeditions from Asunción helped found several other colonial settlements in the region.

♡ From Asunción, Maud took a 24-hour bus to Santa Cruz.

04

Bolivia

Lowlands, valleys, salt, mines and the Altiplano

≈ 2,504 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

18
1,014 km from the previous point

Santa Cruz de la Sierra

Founded in 1561, Santa Cruz moved several times before settling in its current location. During the twentieth century it grew from a relatively isolated eastern city into Bolivia’s largest urban economy. Its rapid modern growth made it one of the strongest contrasts in the journey: low altitude, humid heat and sprawling flat streets after the southern cone and before the Andes.

Little local gem ✦ the tropical lowland climate makes Santa Cruz feel dramatically different from the Andean Bolivia many travellers expect.

19
86 km from the previous point

Samaipata

Samaipata sits where the Andes meet Bolivia’s eastern lowlands. Nearby El Fuerte preserves a major ceremonial complex used by pre-Inca societies and later the Inca. Because it sits between very different ecological zones, Samaipata has long functioned as a meeting point between highland and lowland worlds.

Little local gem ✦ El Fuerte contains a huge carved sandstone rock and is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

20
173 km from the previous point

Sucre

Founded as La Plata in 1538, Sucre became the judicial and intellectual centre of Charcas. It remains Bolivia’s constitutional capital. Its role in the independence era remains visible in civic buildings and museums, while the university tradition gives the city a strong intellectual identity.

Little local gem ✦ the whitewashed historic centre is so distinctive that Sucre is commonly called the ‘White City’.

21
274 km from the previous point

Tupiza

Tupiza lies in a dry valley surrounded by vividly coloured rock formations in southern Bolivia. The region’s mining routes connected it historically with Potosí and Argentina. The red cliffs and eroded formations around town give the valley an almost cinematic landscape that looks very different from the white salt and open plateau farther north.

Little local gem ✦ local tradition links the surrounding region to the final movements of the outlaws Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid.

22
159 km from the previous point

Uyuni

Uyuni developed as a railway and mining town on Bolivia’s southern Altiplano and became the gateway to Salar de Uyuni. The town itself grew from railways and mining, but today almost every road, hostel and tour route points toward the enormous salt landscape outside it.

Little local gem ✦ Salar de Uyuni is the world’s largest salt flat, covering more than 10,000 square kilometres.

23
149 km from the previous point

Potosí

Potosí became one of the richest and largest cities in the world after huge silver deposits were exploited at Cerro Rico from the sixteenth century onward. For centuries, silver from Cerro Rico moved through global trade networks and helped finance the Spanish Empire, while the human cost of extracting it was immense.

Little local gem ✦ the phrase ‘vale un Potosí’ entered Spanish as a way of describing something of enormous value.

24
248 km from the previous point

Cochabamba

Cochabamba developed in a fertile Andean valley that supplied food to mining centres such as Potosí. The city later became a major agricultural and commercial centre. Its broad valley, milder climate and agricultural tradition give it a very different rhythm from the colder highland cities on either side of it.

Little local gem ✦ Cochabamba is famous within Bolivia for its food culture and unusually generous portion sizes.

25
92 km from the previous point

Torotoro

Torotoro is a small Andean town beside a national park of canyons, caves, folded rock formations and fossil beds. The surrounding terrain records millions of years of geological history in folded mountains, deep canyons and fossilised tracks visible directly in the rock.

Little local gem ✦ the park contains thousands of visible dinosaur footprints from the Cretaceous period.

26
309 km from the previous point

La Paz

La Paz was founded in 1548 and moved to the valley of Chuquiago Marka soon afterward. Its steep geography produced one of the most visually distinctive urban landscapes in the world. The city climbs dramatically from the lower valley toward El Alto, so altitude, architecture and social geography change visibly as you move upward.

Little local gem ✦ Mi Teleférico created the world’s largest urban cable-car network, connecting neighbourhoods across enormous changes in altitude.

05

Peru

Inca roads, canyon, desert and high mountains

≈ 2,498 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

27
528 km from the previous point

Cusco

Cusco was the political and ceremonial centre of the Inca Empire. After the Spanish conquest, colonial churches and houses were built directly over monumental Inca stonework. Spanish plazas and churches were inserted into an Inca capital whose walls, street alignments and sacred geography never entirely disappeared.

Little local gem ✦ the famous twelve-angled stone in the historic centre shows the extraordinary precision of Inca masonry.

28
323 km from the previous point

Arequipa

Arequipa was founded as a Spanish city in 1540 in a valley occupied long before colonial rule. Its historic centre is built largely from pale volcanic sillar. Repeated earthquakes shaped both the city’s architecture and its rebuilding, while the pale volcanic stone gives the historic centre a very distinct light.

Little local gem ✦ three volcanoes — Misti, Chachani and Pichu Pichu — dominate the city’s skyline.

29
96 km from the previous point

Colca Canyon

The Colca Valley has been intensively farmed for centuries, with pre-Inca terraces covering its steep slopes. The canyon became one of southern Peru’s best-known natural landscapes. Communities continue farming ancient terraces along the valley, so the landscape is both monumental and intensely lived-in rather than simply a natural viewpoint.

Little local gem ✦ Cruz del Cóndor is famous for sightings of Andean condors riding the canyon’s morning thermal currents.

30
281 km from the previous point

Inca Trail · Machu Picchu

The classic Inca Trail follows part of the vast Andean road system through mountain passes and archaeological sites before reaching Machu Picchu. The route matters because the archaeological sites appear gradually along the trail, making the final arrival at Machu Picchu part of a much larger journey rather than an isolated destination.

Little local gem ✦ the classic route is about 43 km long and traditionally reaches Machu Picchu through Inti Punku, the Sun Gate.

♡ Maud completed the Inca Trail.

31
329 km from the previous point

Nazca Lines

The Nazca and Palpa desert preserves hundreds of giant geoglyphs created roughly between 500 BCE and 500 CE. The dryness of the desert helped preserve the lines for centuries, leaving enormous geometric forms and figures etched into an otherwise seemingly empty plain.

Little local gem ✦ many figures are so large that their full shapes are easiest to understand from the air.

32
157 km from the previous point

Paracas

Paracas is a desert peninsula on Peru’s Pacific coast and gives its name to an important pre-Hispanic culture. The surrounding national reserve protects desert, islands and rich marine ecosystems. The contrast is striking: almost rainless desert cliffs sit immediately beside one of the richest marine environments on the Peruvian coast.

Little local gem ✦ the Paracas Candelabra, an enormous geoglyph cut into a coastal hillside, is visible from the sea.

♡ At the bus office, the ticket seller told Maud: “mañana en la mañana.”

33
499 km from the previous point

Huaraz

Huaraz lies in the Callejón de Huaylas beneath the Cordillera Blanca. Much of the modern city was rebuilt after the devastating 1970 Ancash earthquake. It is the main gateway to the Cordillera Blanca, where turquoise glacial lakes and extremely high peaks sit unusually close to towns in the valley.

Little local gem ✦ nearby Huascarán, at 6,768 metres, is Peru’s highest mountain.

34
285 km from the previous point

Lima

Founded in 1535 as the City of Kings, Lima became the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru and one of Spanish America’s most important cities. Its location between desert and Pacific Ocean shaped a city whose food, architecture and climate are very different from the Andean interior.

Little local gem ✦ Lima receives very little rain despite spending much of the year under a cool coastal fog known as garúa.

06

Brazil

Down the Atlantic coast

≈ 4,634 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

35
3,779 km from the previous point

Rio de Janeiro

Rio was founded in 1565, later became the seat of the Portuguese monarchy in the Americas, and served as Brazil’s capital until 1960. Few cities combine dense urban life with such dramatic topography: granite peaks, rainforest, bays and beaches continually interrupt the street grid.

Little local gem ✦ the city’s dramatic meeting of mountains, forest and sea is recognised by UNESCO as a cultural landscape.

36
112 km from the previous point

Ilha Grande

Ilha Grande spent centuries relatively isolated from large-scale development and was once used for quarantine stations and prisons. Today much of the island is protected Atlantic Forest. The absence of large-scale road traffic helped preserve a slower island rhythm, with beaches and settlements still connected largely by boats and forest paths.

Little local gem ✦ there are no regular private cars in the island’s main settlements; boats and walking trails connect much of the coast.

37
50 km from the previous point

Paraty

Paraty grew as a colonial port on the route carrying gold from Minas Gerais to the Atlantic. Its preserved centre combines Portuguese colonial architecture with an extraordinary coastal mountain setting. The old port’s streets, churches and houses survived unusually intact, while forested mountains rise immediately behind the colonial centre.

Little local gem ✦ parts of the historic centre were designed to flood naturally at high tide, which helped wash the old streets.

38
45 km from the previous point

Ubatuba

Ubatuba sits between the Serra do Mar and the Atlantic and has a long Indigenous and Portuguese colonial history. It is now known for its beaches and surviving Atlantic Forest. Its long coastline and heavy Atlantic rainfall support one of the greenest stretches of the São Paulo coast, where forest often reaches almost to the beach.

Little local gem ✦ the municipality has more than 100 named beaches along its coastline.

39
159 km from the previous point

São Paulo

São Paulo began around a Jesuit mission founded in 1554. Coffee, immigration, railways and industrialisation transformed it into Brazil’s largest metropolis. Successive waves of immigration transformed its food, neighbourhoods and industry, turning it into one of the most culturally diverse cities in the hemisphere.

Little local gem ✦ Avenida Paulista closes much of its roadway to cars on Sundays and becomes a huge pedestrian public space.

40
489 km from the previous point

Florianópolis

Florianópolis developed around Santa Catarina Island, Indigenous settlement and later strong Azorean migration. The modern city spreads across island and mainland. The island combines dense city neighbourhoods with fishing villages, dunes, lagoons and long stretches of beach, often only a short drive apart.

Little local gem ✦ the island is often said to have 42 beaches, though local counts vary depending on what is considered a separate beach.

07

Colombia

High plateau, Sierra Nevada and Caribbean islands

≈ 5,338 km added to the mapped route in this chapter

42
4,258 km from the previous point

Bogotá

Bogotá stands on the high Andean plateau once occupied by the Muisca and became the Spanish centre of New Granada after its foundation in 1538. The historic centre, steep eastern mountains and enormous modern city all sit on the same plateau, giving Bogotá a scale that is difficult to understand until you are inside it.

Little local gem ✦ at about 2,640 metres above sea level, Bogotá is one of the world’s highest large capital cities.

43
35 km from the previous point

Zipaquirá

Zipaquirá grew around salt deposits that had been exploited long before the Spanish arrived. Salt remained central to the town’s economy for centuries. Salt shaped the economy here long before the colonial era, and the underground cathedral turned that mining history into one of Colombia’s most unusual architectural spaces.

Little local gem ✦ the famous Salt Cathedral is built inside former mine tunnels, deep within a halite mountain.

44
692 km from the previous point

Santa Marta

Founded in 1525, Santa Marta is one of the oldest surviving Spanish-founded cities in South America. It sits between the Caribbean and the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta. Its location is extraordinary: Caribbean beaches lie immediately below an isolated mountain system that contains some of the highest peaks in Colombia.

Little local gem ✦ the Sierra Nevada rises from the Caribbean coast to snow-covered peaks over 5,000 metres high in a remarkably short horizontal distance.

45
37 km from the previous point

Lost City Trek · Teyuna

Teyuna, widely known as Ciudad Perdida, was built by Tairona communities centuries before the Spanish conquest. Its stone terraces and pathways are hidden in the Sierra Nevada rainforest. The journey to the terraces crosses rivers, humid forest and Indigenous territories, so the archaeological site is inseparable from the landscape surrounding it.

Little local gem ✦ reaching the archaeological site still requires several days of hiking; there is no road access.

♡ Maud completed the Lost City trek.

46
46 km from the previous point

Palomino

Palomino is a small Caribbean settlement between the sea and the Sierra Nevada, within a region shaped by Indigenous territories, rivers and coastal trade. Rivers descend from the Sierra Nevada almost directly to the Caribbean here, creating a landscape where mountain water and tropical coastline meet within only a few kilometres.

Little local gem ✦ on very clear days, it is possible to experience tropical beach weather while seeing the high Sierra Nevada in the distance.

47
62 km from the previous point

Minca

Minca lies in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada above Santa Marta and developed around farms and coffee estates in a cooler mountain climate. Its cooler air, coffee farms, waterfalls and forest made it a natural retreat from the much hotter Caribbean coast below.

Little local gem ✦ its altitude makes it noticeably cooler than the Caribbean coast only a short distance below.

48
171 km from the previous point

Cartagena de Indias

Founded in 1533, Cartagena became one of the Spanish Empire’s most important fortified Caribbean ports. Its walls and forts preserve the history of Atlantic trade, conflict and slavery. The old city became wealthy because of its strategic port, and the massive walls around it still make the colonial centre feel unusually self-contained.

Little local gem ✦ the city’s fortification system includes Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, one of the largest Spanish military complexes in the Americas.

49
37 km from the previous point

Isla Grande · Rosario Islands

Isla Grande is part of the Rosario Islands, a Caribbean archipelago southwest of Cartagena surrounded by coral reefs and mangrove ecosystems. The island landscape mixes Caribbean water, coral habitat, mangroves and small settlements, giving the final coastal stretch a very different scale from Cartagena itself.

Little local gem ✦ much of the archipelago lies within the Rosario and San Bernardo Corals National Natural Park.

≈

Mangrove tour

One last Caribbean experience before the route looped south again: Maud went on a mangrove tour, moving through one of the coastal ecosystems that make this part of the Caribbean so different from the open sea.

Little local gem ✦ Mangroves act as nurseries for fish and crustaceans, while their dense roots help protect tropical coastlines from waves and erosion.

The end of this map

What a way to cross a continent.

The route began in Santiago, crossed mountains, desert, jungle, islands and coastlines, returned to Santiago for a few more days, and finally ended in Cartagena before Amsterdam.

One last loop

Back to Santiago. Then Cartagena.

After the mangrove tour, Maud returned to Santiago for a few more days before the final leg of the journey.

50
The route turns south again

Santiago de Chile · one more return

After months of moving through the continent, Santiago appeared once more — this time for a few days before the final departure.

♡ A few more days in Santiago before the journey moved north one last time.

51
The final Latin American stop

Cartagena · departure for Amsterdam

From Santiago, Maud returned to Cartagena. The Caribbean city became the final geographic point of the journey in Latin America — the place from which she would take her flight to Amsterdam.

Little local gem ✦ Cartagena’s old walled city was built around one of the most important Caribbean ports of the Spanish Empire, so ending the journey here means finishing in a city that has been a departure point for centuries.

Cartagena → Amsterdam
